Claude took its first shot at an antivenom Scorpions sting more than 1.2 million people a year. The antivenom still comes from horses injected with venom, and it takes months to produce. Anthropic had Claude design an alternative from scratch. 64 hours, five human messages, 318,484 candidate designs for proteins that grab scorpion toxins before they reach your nerves. 211 went to Twist Bioscience and Adaptyv Bio for testing. 17 bound to the toxin they were built for. The best two grab a Mexican scorpion's toxin in roughly the same spot as an antibody already known to protect mice. Claude emailed the lab with its own questions mid-run, then kept designing when the answers came back. The team running it was Citrini Research, an investment research firm.  Five staffers, most with no science background, working from Anthropic's offices because they couldn't get the safety block lifted on their own machines. $49,997 on compute, three dollars under budget, plus about $150,000 on lab work. What it isn't: each of the 17 binds one toxin, and nobody has tested whether they actually stop the venom. No cells, no animals yet. Citrini called its universal antivenom moonshot a failure. Its own conclusion was that the frontier has moved. That's an honest read. The result is a set of binders rather than a drug. The new thing here is the team.
